entry.title: FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1612
entry.content:
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.

Key holding: Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

entry.title: Ms Erica Bosloper v Linkpoint Lawyers Pty Ltd & Mr Jun Pan [2026] FWC 4208
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4208, the Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection by Linkpoint Lawyers Pty Ltd and Jun Pan to Erica Bosloper’s s 365 application, contending she was not an employee and therefore could not have been dismissed. The Commission examined the written “Partnership Agreement” and how it was performed in practice, and found she was an employee dismissed on the employer’s initiative. The objection was dismissed.

Key holding: Under s 15AA, whether a person is an employee is determined by the real substance, practical reality and true nature of the relationship, considering the totality including actual performance, and is not controlled by the parties’ expressed intention or contractual label.

But the analysis required by section 15AA is not confined to the parties' intentions, or to the terms by which they recorded their intentions. This is made clear in the section itself, as confirmed in the authorities to which I have referred.

entry.title: Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1620
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.

Key holding: Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: Mrs Kristie Maggar v Laura Brown [2026] FWC 4197
entry.content:
LN Veterinary sought costs after Ms Maggar discontinued her unfair dismissal application. The Fair Work Commission refused costs under s 611(2), but ordered $980.75 under s 400A for unreasonable procedural conduct concerning a late adjournment request and failure to instruct her lawyer. Key holding: Under s 400A, costs may be ordered where a party’s unreasonable act or omission in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter caused the other party to incur costs.

The FWC may make an order for costs against a party to a matter arising under this Part (the first party) for costs incurred by the other party to the matter if the FWC is satisfied that the first party caused those costs to be incurred because of an unreasonable act or omission of the first party in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter.

entry.title: United Firefighters' Union of Australia (259V) v Triple Zero Victoria [2026] FWC 4199
entry.content:
The UFU applied under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Commission to determine whether a TZV employee was entitled to an independent investigator for serious misconduct allegations. The Commission held that neither the Triple Zero Victoria Operations Enterprise Agreement 2024 nor the TZV Workplace Investigations Procedure created that entitlement. It nonetheless recommended that Mr Walker proceed as TZV’s appointed investigator.

Key holding: Clause 67.4 requires any summary dismissal to be carried out in accordance with TZV policies and procedures consistent with the FW Act and Regulations, but it does not incorporate those policies into the Agreement or create a pre-dismissal entitlement to an independent investigation.

Properly construed, in my view, what the clause commits the Respondent to do is to enact the "summary dismissal of any employee" in accordance with its policies and procedures which must be consistent with the provisions of the Act and FW Regulations.

entry.title: CFMEU (105N) v Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Pty Ltd Trading AS Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal [2026] FWC 4200
entry.content:
The FWC determined a dispute under the Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Stevedoring Enterprise Agreement 2021–2025 about whether Mr Conway was entitled to permanent reclassification from Grade 3 to Grade 5. It held the 70% higher-duty threshold is a gateway only, not a mandatory entitlement, and that FACT’s refusal was consistent with the Agreement because it applied permissible merit/conduct considerations under cl 26.5.4.

Key holding: Meeting the 70% higher-duty threshold under cl 26.5.3 only permits an application and does not entitle an employee to permanent reclassification; once the gateway is met, the employer may refuse on merit principles relating to the employee’s performance, attendance, conduct or attitude.

once an employee meets the threshold of having worked seventy per cent of shifts for which they are available at a higher grade over the previous twelve months they can apply for a permanent r eclassification. Once the employee submits their application in accordance with the provisions of clause 26.5.1 and 26.5.2, the Respondent can apply merit principles as they relate to the performance or conduct of the employee to determine if the reclassification will be granted.

entry.title: Prabhatkumar Valabhai Zala v Shred-X Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4204
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Zala’s s.394 unfair dismissal application after Shred-X objected that he was not dismissed. Mr Zala resigned after a manager’s inappropriate comment and a period of psychological injury, but the Commission found Shred-X did not force him to resign. The application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction under s.386 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Key holding: Whether a resignation was forced is assessed objectively by reference to the employer’s conduct, not the employee’s subjective feeling.

It is the conduct of the employer that must be assessed, not whether the employee subjectively felt like they were forced to resign.

entry.title: Claire Lin v Compass Group Remote Hospitality Services Pty Ltd & Anne Richardson and Another [2026] FWC 4201
entry.content:
Ms Lin applied under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging she was dismissed after receiving an email about her fixed-term contract ending. The employer objected that she remained employed and had not been dismissed. The Commission upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A mistaken communication about a fixed-term contract ending does not amount to dismissal under s 386 where the employer has not terminated the employment relationship and the employee remains employed.

Noting that I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the contract of employment on 8 May 2026, further, I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the employment relationship. Ms Lin remained employed by the Respondent, and I am satisfied that she remains employed.

entry.title: Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2501
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

entry.title: Bhardwaj and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation) [2026] ARTA 2482
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a self-represented taxpayer’s objection decision concerning deductions for work-related car, travel, clothing, self-education, other expenses, gifts and tax affairs, plus interest on money borrowed to buy shares. It disallowed most deductions and held the interest was capital and not deductible, but allowed $67,500 as the third element of the cost base of the shares. The objection decision was varied accordingly.

Key holding: Interest under a bona fide loan is incurred in the income year it becomes due and payable and may be included in the third element of the cost base even if not paid.

The Tribunal expressed its view that, consistent with the established principle as expressed in Federal Commissioner of Taxation v James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65; (1953) 88 CLR 492, the interest became due and payable in the 2020 - 21 income year and, accordingly, the balance of $67,500 was, if shown to be deductable or otherwise allowable in the cost base, deductible or allowable in its entirety in the 2020 - 21 income year.
